newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Aid workers fear all-out war in eastern Zaire.
newsitem.headline: Aid workers fear all-out war in eastern Zaire.

text.p: Aid workers said on Wednesday they feared all-out war in eastern Zaire after a one-week ultimatum from Zairean authorities for an estimated 200,000 ethnic Tutsis to leave.
"We fear there will be a fully-fledged war with helicopter gunships and heavy arms being used by the Zaireans after the people leave," said an aid worker in the eastern border town of Bukavu.
"The situation is explosive," added a U.N. official.
South Kivu Deputy Governor Lwasi Ngabo Lwabanji issued the ultimatum on Tuesday and told a news conference in Bukavu the Banyamulenge Tutsis were bent on destabilising eastern Zaire.
He said rebels, with hundreds of thousands of Banyamulenge civilians living in the plateau area of South Kivu, had a week to leave or face all-out war from the Zairean defence forces.
He said any Banyamulenge failing to heed his warning within seven days would be considered rebels and attacked by troops.
"We are opening a corridor for the Banyamulenge who want to get out for one week. After that whoever remains will be considered a rebel and will be treated as such," he said.

Conflict between the army and estimated 200,000 Banyamulenge has been growing for months. The Banyamulenge are ethnic Tutsis who arrived up to 200 years ago from what are now neighbouring Rwanda and Burundi.

Zairean authorities have whipped up public opinion against the Banyamulenge and diplomats fear conflict could spread as the mainly Tutsi armies in Rwanda and Burundi may decide to support their kinfolk.

It was unclear whether aid agencies would cooperate with a Zairean request for them to supervise a "corridor" so civilians could gather in villages on the eastern shore of Lake Tanganyika bordering on Rwanda.
Zairean authorities want to concentrate the Banyamulenge in government-controlled camps to make them easier to monitor.
Aid workers said Banyamulenge armed groups and the Zairean army were already fighting a war on a plateau south of Bukavu.
"The people on the plateau who were fighting will carry on fighting. On Tuesday the Zaireans just made it official and now everybody on the plateau knows the truth," an aid worker said.
On Tuesday Bukavu was shaken by more than an hour of automatic gunfire by Zairean troops after the bodies of an army colonel and seven soldiers killed in fighting with Banyamulenge arrived in town.
Aid workers said soldiers in vehicles fired their weapons in the town and there was a small amount of looting from shops.
Lwabanji said Banyamulenge rebels attacked the town of Lemera mid-way between Bukavu and the town of Uvira on Sunday, killing all patients and medical staff. He gave no death toll.

A U.N. official confirmed the attack on the 360-bed Lemera hospital, one of the best in the region, saying armed men said to be Banyamulenge killed patients, damaged a generator and set a fire in a garage.
"It appears to have been a hit-and-run attack," he said.
Zairean soldiers went on a looting rampage in Uvira town for about four hours on Tuesday, robbing foreign aid workers at gunpoint and stealing at least two aid vehicles, residents said.
Zaire's army is notoriously indisciplined. Soldiers say their pay is a pittance and they turn to crime to survive.
But their commander-in-chief, President Mobutu Sese Seko, is not in the country to impose his limited authority. Mobutu is in Switzerland after surgery with no firm date for his return.
